intro: Leopold Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra play the third movement of Scheherazade, Op. 35, “The Young Prince and the Young Princess”, which opens with a long G-major violin tune accompanied by quick woodwind runs. This 1934 recording contains only the opening disc side.

sections.label: A · Violin melody in G major
sections.mNote: Long violin melody over sustained lower strings.

sections.label: B · woodwind figures around the string melody
sections.mNote: Small wind figures surround the longer string phrases.

sections.label: C · Melody shared by winds and strings
sections.mNote: The melody passes between different instruments of the orchestra.

sections.label: D · Last phrases on this side
sections.mNote: The disc ends partway through the movement.

cues.title: Opening theme, violins
cues.text: The violins begin in G major above held lower strings. Their tune alternates long notes with short, quick runs. Rimsky-Korsakov marked the movement Andantino quasi allegretto.
cues.evidence: Full score, third movement, printed p. 54, opening Andantino quasi allegretto. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0f/IMSLP01398-Rimsky_Sheherazade_3.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Philadelphia, November 1934
cues.text: On 12 November 1934 Stokowski recorded Scheherazade with the Philadelphia Orchestra. This side holds the beginning of the third movement. The label gives the tempo, Andantino quasi allegretto, and calls it ‘Part 1’.
cues.evidence: Recording date, performers and side description on the source record. https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=File:Hmv-db2525-2a84519.ogg

cues.title: Woodwind decorations around the string melody
cues.text: Quick woodwind decorations accompany the string melody. A run passes while the tune holds one note, and then the longer phrase resumes. The instruments move at different speeds within the same pulse.
cues.evidence: Full score, third movement, opening section, printed pp. 54–58: violin melody, clarinet runs and wind replies. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0f/IMSLP01398-Rimsky_Sheherazade_3.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First release on disc, 1935
cues.text: The recording was first issued in 1935 on short sides. This side holds Part 1 of the third movement and stops before the movement’s ending. The next side continues the lovers’ music up to the return of Scheherazade’s solo violin and the close.
cues.evidence: Source record gives first release in 1935 and identifies this as Part 1 of the third movement; full score, printed pp. 66–75, contains the later violin recitative and close. https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=File:Hmv-db2525-2a84519.ogg

composer.epithet: Russian composer and professor, known for fairy-tale operas and his detailed knowledge of the orchestra; he became a professor before he had learned counterpoint.
facts: Naval College, Saint Petersburg; composition with Balakirev and years of private study
Conservatory professor from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Fifteen operas, from The Maid of Pskov to The Golden Cockerel
composer.background:
Before he had seen the sea, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov rigged a toy brig and read letters from his older brother Voyin, a naval officer. Growing up in Tikhvin, he wanted a ship of his own. His father took him to the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856, and his piano lessons continued alongside his naval education. In 1861 his teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Mily Balakirev, who encouraged the seventeen-year-old cadet to begin a symphony.

The clipper Almaz carried him away in 1862 on a voyage of nearly three years. During a long stop in England he wrote the symphony’s slow movement without a piano, and took a chance to try it at a restaurant. He posted the music to Balakirev, who replied with encouragement and requests for changes. Farther out, he saw the Gulf Stream turn the ocean blue, flying fish and phosphorescence. After his return to Russia he took up music again, and Balakirev conducted the completed First Symphony in December 1865.
